food.text: No agricultural revolution took place in the Arabian Peninsula during the early Holocene, unlike much of the rest of the Fertile Crescent. Instead, nomadic pastoralism continued to characterize the region for thousands of years.

The Neolithic Al-Magar culture, centered in southwestern Najd in what is now Saudi Arabia, was one of the first communities in the world to practice agriculture and animal husbandry. Its people lived in stone houses built with dry masonry.

Dilmun, a civilization spanning what are now Bahrain, Kuwait, and eastern Saudi Arabia, became an important trading center controlling Persian Gulf trade routes from the late fourth millennium BC onward. It lay on a trade route between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, close to the sea and artesian springs.

The people of Al-Magar lived in stone houses built with dry masonry. They were one of the first communities in the world to practise agriculture and animal husbandry, before climate changes in the region led to desertification.

A large statue of a bridled horse found at Al-Magar suggests that horses were domesticated there about 9,000 years ago, making it possibly one of the earliest sites of horse domestication in the world. This is much earlier than horse domestication is thought to have occurred elsewhere.

Even though no agricultural revolution took place within Arabia itself, its nomadic populations still interacted with the agricultural and sedentary communities of neighboring regions during this era. This kept Arabia's herders in contact with farming societies nearby.

Ubaid pottery made in Mesopotamia began reaching the Persian Gulf coast of Arabia toward the end of the sixth millennium BC, with finds at sites such as Dosariyah in Saudi Arabia. The pottery's presence peaked around 5300 BC and is thought to have been a valuable trade item rather than just a container for other goods.

Al-Magar's early practice of agriculture and animal husbandry eventually came to an end when climate change caused desertification in the region. This climatic shift altered the environment that had once supported the region's farming and herding communities.

Because Ubaid pottery reaching the Arabian side of the Persian Gulf coast seems to have been traded for its own value, archaeologists are unsure exactly what was exchanged for it. Suggested possibilities include dates and other foodstuffs, semi-precious materials, jewelry, animal products, and livestock.

At Dosariyah on Arabia's Persian Gulf coast, local potters also made pottery that imitated imported Ubaid wares from Mesopotamia. This reinforces the idea that the Mesopotamian pottery was a valued trade item along the Gulf coast.

art.text: At Al-Magar, a Neolithic culture in southwestern Najd in Saudi Arabia, archaeologists found a large statue of a bridled horse. The find indicates that horses were domesticated in the Arabian peninsula about 9000 years ago, much earlier than in other parts of the world where horse domestication is thought to have occurred.

Neolithic artifacts found in Hail Province date from 10000 BC to 7500 BC. What sets Hail apart from other parts of Saudi Arabia is the abundance of its rock drawings, which show both human and animal figures.

The Rock Art in the Ha'il Region is the fourth site in Saudi Arabia to be inscribed on the UNESCO List of World Heritage Sites. Its petroglyphs, carved into rock surfaces by an ancient population, hold 8,000 years of history.

Recent Arabian archaeology has uncovered thousands of years of rock art in the Al-Ula region. It has also found monumental stone structures at the Al Ha'it Oasis, showing how much creative work still lies in the peninsula's deserts.

Shell middens on Oman's western coast, dated to about the middle of the fifth to the third millennium BCE, held graves with simple jewelry. Shell beads turn up along the coast into the UAE, and some shells not native to the UAE suggest trade between communities.

Neolithic Hail is marked by varied environments, from the sandy banks of valleys to dune slopes and ancient lake deposits, including those at Jubbah. Stone tools suggest that the people who made the region's rock drawings lived by hunting and gathering rather than in permanent settlements.

Around 5500 BC, the Copper Age in Hail Province left stone formations and circles. Together with flint tools, vessels of rough, unpolished clay and rock inscriptions, they show that life was more settled than the hunting and gathering of the Neolithic.

Copper Age craftspeople in Hail Province made stone tools with flat sides. These took the form of scrapers, drills and cleavers, and they are among the most widespread cultural evidence from about 5500 BC in the region.

A 2010 study by Tara Steimer-Herbet in the book Roads of Arabia is titled "Three Funerary Stelae from the 4th Millennium BC". Its title points to carved funerary monuments from Arabia in the fourth millennium BC.

science.text: The Bronze Age began on the Arabian Peninsula in the late fourth millennium BC. The transition profoundly altered Arabian societies by introducing metallurgy and the use of metals for all sorts of tasks.

The Neolithic began 11,700 years ago with the advent of agriculture, but no agricultural revolution took place in the Arabian Peninsula in the early Holocene. Arabian populations did interact with farming and sedentary peoples, yet nomadic pastoralism continued to characterize the region for thousands of years.

Al-Magar was an advanced Neolithic culture centered in modern-day southwestern Najd in Saudi Arabia. It is possibly one of the first cultures in the world where widespread domestication of animals occurred, particularly the horse.
Between 11,000 and 6,000 years ago, Arabia saw a large population expansion. Archaeologists infer it from a large increase in the number of known settlements dating to this period.

By 6,000 years ago the Arabian economy had transitioned to nomadic pastoralism. It is still debated whether this spread through the migration of Levantine peoples, who already practiced it, or was an internal development that came from trade with the Levant.

culture.text: Unlike much of the Fertile Crescent, Arabia saw no agricultural revolution in the early Holocene, though its people did interact with farming and settled communities. Instead, nomadic pastoralism continued to characterize the region for thousands of years.

From about 10,000 BCE, Arabia's early Holocene rock art included rare, life-sized, highly naturalistic engravings of wild animals. Subjects included wild camels, African wild ass with shoulder stripes, ibex and aurochs.

When the Bronze Age began in Arabia in the late fourth millennium BC, metallurgy entered society and metals were used for all sorts of tasks. Around this time sanctuaries first appeared, starting a long tradition in the religious history of the region.

From much of the fourth millennium BC into parts of the third (roughly 5900 to 5300 years ago), Arabia went through a prolonged phase of extreme aridity called the Dark Millennium. It followed earlier humid Holocene conditions, and lakes, wetlands and vegetation contracted. In southeastern Arabia, which lacked groundwater, people abandoned the interior deserts on a large scale and moved to the Persian Gulf coast. Even there, archaeological evidence suggests the coastal communities suffered nutritional stress.

The early Holocene animal engravings were often detailed with eyes, muscles and coat patterns. They tended to cluster near water sources along escarpments, and they show no human figures or interactions.
Regions such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have very few archaeological sites from the Dark Millennium. The period also coincides with the decline of Ubaid cultures.
Some archaeologists consider much of the Arabian Peninsula to have been abandoned during the Dark Millennium. Recent research instead suggests that the picture varied from region to region.
